items.body: Hear a voice call through the trees Leave this dying world behind Come along and follow me To the meadows of our minds A good fairy tale knows that beauty can get you into trouble, and that an invitation to dance may come with terms and conditions nobody bothered to explain. For Washington, D.C.’s Faeryn Johnson, the musician behind Faded Pulse, that uneasy invitation opens onto Elysia, a second album where ethereal wave, goth, folk, and dream pop meet the romantic imagination of medieval poetry and Victorian painting. Acoustic guitars, hammered dulcimer, electric bass, and ambient synthesizers accompany water spirits, waiting maidens, and woodland gatherings whose hosts have questionable intentions. The route here runs through the synthpop of 2025’s Submission and the more ethereal leanings of that year’s Fallen EP, with a decisive turn taken while watching Monica Richards perform with Strange Boutique in Washington. Johnson’s affection for the 1990s Projekt catalogue supplies another set of coordinates: Lycia, Love Spirals Downwards, Black Tape for a Blue Girl, and Unto Ashes sit alongside the folk of Pentangle and Donovan. There is a generous curiosity at work, the kind that can find room for both a Slowdive bassline and a William Morris poem without making either feel like an unlikely guest. Johnson’s background in art history gives Elysia a visual life as rich as its musical references. Waterhouse’s paintings, the Arts and Crafts movement, and Art Nouveau belong to the same imaginative world as thrifted velvet, medieval dress, and an old copy of Tennyson found in an antique shop. Beneath the finery lie practical questions about courage, community, and how to remain attentive to the living world. This gathering of fairies may be perilous, but the hope is that listeners return from it with a renewed appetite for their own lives. We spoke with Johnson about the records that opened those doors, the literature and paintings behind Elysia, and the enduring possibilities of ethereal music, from a hammered dulcimer to a dream performance among the art and architecture of the Cloisters. Before Faded Pulse, what first opened the door to the Gothic imagination for you? Was there a particular record, book, painting, or encounter that made you feel you had found somewhere you belonged? Faded Pulse: I started getting into the gothic scene when I was around 14 years old, and at that time my most essential record was The Cure’s Pornography. I loved the dense, almost psychedelic sound of the album. I’ve probably overplayed that record way too much at that age. Yet it really cemented my love for atmosphere and dense sound design. Robert Smith’s honest and vulnerable lyricism made me feel so seen and got me through so much. Between Submission, Fallen, and Elysia, your music has moved further into folk and ethereal wave. What was happening in your life and listening habits that encouraged that change, and what could you express through these arrangements that you hadn’t explored before? Faded Pulse: When I first started “Submission” around 2022, I was very much into the New Wave and Synthpop sounds of the 80s, and that really shows on that album, although my listening has always been more eclectic. One big influence on Elysia was psych and folk of the 60s and 70s, particularly bands like Pentangle; their album Solomon’s Seal was super influential on me, especially songs like “Willy O’Winsbury”. Donovan was another big influence; you can really hear it on songs like “Will Thy Heart Be True,” where I go for a more folky, ballad-type song. I have always had a huge love for the 90’s ethereal scene. The moment I knew I wanted to move sonically towards that was when I saw Strange Boutique live at the Black Cat in D.C. in 2025. Seeing Monica Richards on stage and hearing the music live was really a light-bulb moment for me. Ethereal allows me to experiment more with unusual instrumentation and also lets the music take people to another world. Although I enjoyed making synth pop, here I can play with classical, folk, ambient, and even more rock-oriented structures. It’s so much more playful and freeing. I feel like Faded Pulse would have been a perfect fit for Projekt Festival, especially the 1997 edition. How were you first introduced to the label and its artists, and was there a particular band or record that sparked your affinity for that strain of ethereal music? Faded Pulse: Projekt has a special place in my heart and is probably one of my favorite labels ever. My essential four artists from the record label are Black Tape, Lycia, Love Spirals, and Unto Ashes. Black Tape for a Blue Girl’s “Remnants of a Deeper Purity” is one of my all-time favs; it is a masterpiece in its own right in sound design and atmosphere, and it’s both deeply haunting and romantic. I feel like Love Spirals Downwards Idylls is glaringly obvious as one of the influences on Elysia, and I feel it is their most essential record. It’s hard for me to choose a Lycia album because they’re my favorite band on the label, but if I had to choose, it would be “A Day in the Stark Corner”. It’s equal parts dreamy, cold, and bleak. Unto Ashes serves everything I look for in a band: medieval instruments and sounds, folk and darkwave synths. I feel like their album “Empty into white” is so sonically rich and put together, sinister yet dreamy. I’m not sure how I even stumbled on the label, which feels fitting, like it came to me almost in a dream; it is the most influential group of artists for me. There’s something about Elysia that feels entirely at home in the pages of Propaganda or Carpe Noctem. What feels special to you about the Gothic culture of the ’90s, and how have you encountered that period through its music, magazines, photography, and fashion? Faded Pulse: Funnily enough, I own an issue of Propaganda, No. 22, and I wanna say it’s from 1994-1996. I have very fond memories of reading Propaganda magazines in high school on the Internet Archive. I am a historian at heart and love to learn everything I can about culture, music, and fashions of any time period I study. The 90’s, to me, feel somehow criminally underrated, even though it was when the gothic scene was at its peak and fully found itself and diversified into many different interests. I feel the worship of the 80s has caused people to overlook how creative the scene was in the 90s. Even now, somehow darkwave from the 90s is still more experimental and fresh than the very 80s-oriented sounds we get today. As for the fashion, I would study a lot of the pictures on Pinterest from magazines, club shoots, or people’s personal uploads, and when I went thrifting, I would look for similar items. PVC, Satins, Silks, and Velvet are all mainstays in my closet thanks to the 90s, haha. “Meadow of My Mind” and “Upon the Heavens” feel like a bridge between Cocteau Twins and the more romantic corners of the Projekt catalogue. How do you approach the relationship between voice and guitar in these songs, especially when both seem capable of carrying the melody or dissolving into one another? Faded Pulse: Much like the bands before me, I kind of treat the voice as just another instrument. When recording a lot of these songs, I wanted the guitar and voice to mesh well. In meadow of my mind, the voice and guitar switch throughout the song, giving them space to drive the song along without clashing. In “Meadow of My Mind,” you sing, “Leave this dying world behind,” yet you’ve described Elysia as something beyond escapism. What does that inner refuge make possible for you, and what do you hope listeners bring back from it into their everyday lives? Faded Pulse: To me, “Meadow of my Mind” is about the love of nature, to put it plainly. When listeners “Leave the realm of Elysia,” I want people to bring that sort of magic into their everyday lives. Whether that be getting involved in their local communities, making art, or reading poetry. Whatever it is that makes you feel connected to the world around you. “Upon the Heavens” uses the language of prayer, reaching toward a divine presence and asking to be heard and healed. What is your relationship with that devotional language, and how did you arrive at the kind of sacred experience you wanted the song to convey? Faded Pulse: To me, music is very spiritual, and I definitely wanted Upon the Heavens to emulate that in some way. It’s not a song devoted to a particular deity or religion, but it is about reaching out and feeling something greater. I feel this all the time through music, when I listen to a song that just makes me float away or feel high on euphoria. I mean, historically speaking, music is how people connect to the otherworld and is used in ritual, even though it is now far removed from its sacred roots. Music still feels deeply spiritual and otherworldly, and I think that’s truly what the song conveys. “Lamia’s Kiss” brings to mind Dead Can Dance’s exploration of musical traditions beyond rock, with an experimental quality that feels ancient and unfamiliar at once. Which specific traditions, recordings, or instruments informed it, and how did you develop its musical character? Faded Pulse: The sounds of the Middle East and the Mediterranean very much inspire Lamia’s kiss. A lot of the bands I liked, like Lovespirals, DCD, and Rajna, had eastern influence in their music, so it kinda bled into my consciousness. Rather than writing cliched lyrics about her as a figure, I wanted the song to emulate what it would feel like to be caught in her hypnotic gaze, to be pulled in. Instrumentally, I wanted the Dulcimer to be the lead on the song, which I feel really harnesses that archaic, almost ancient vibe that I wanted the song to have. I also grew up in Asia for a short time. I do think it had a musical effect on me, and it seems only natural that an experience like that would creep into my music in some way. What first drew you to Lamia as a figure? Did you come to her through mythology, Keats’s poem, a painting, or another interpretation, and what interests you about the meeting of beauty, desire, and danger in her story? Faded Pulse: It’s a little bit of all of that. Keats’s poem is definitely an inspo, as is Waterhouse’s iconic painting. I am also a Lilith and Hecate Devotee; the lamia is associated with both, so it’s almost devotional. I also love serpentine imagery and symbolism, as well as the figure of the femme fatale, so it is essentially a collage of many different ideas and feelings. “Fair Lady in Gold” has a baroque richness and a medieval atmosphere, particularly in the bright, struck-string sound that suggests a hammered dulcimer. How did you build that arrangement, and who—or what—is the lady at its center? Faded Pulse: For “Fair Lady in Gold,” I knew I wanted to have a few instrumental tracks on the album. The main instruments here are my Dusty Strings hammered dulcimer and my Korg Minilogue for ambient synths. There is no single song as an influence; rather, months and weeks of studying and listening to music from the Renaissance and medieval period that shaped this song. When I first started writing “The Lady in Gold,” I was envisioning Cordelia from King Lear in a painting by Edwin Austin Abbey. Although her gown is yellow, it is not even close to gold, haha. However, a woman with a golden pooling Bliaut gown was what I was envisioning when creating the song, so the name kinda stuck. “Summerland” seems to occupy a meeting place between Dead Can Dance and Cocteau Twins, while its lyrics describe being drawn into a fairy gathering. How welcoming did you want that invitation to feel, and how much uncertainty or danger belongs within its beauty? Faded Pulse: Summerland is definitely a song where I wanted the listener to be taken away by the fae, where it’s both exhilarating and panic-inducing. To be led away and dancing with beings who look human, yet there is something quite off about them, and strange things happen around them. I wanted to evoke the same feelings I had reading Irish fairy tales, where the stories of the fae are both wondrous and terrifying in equal measure. I think it’s a great metaphor for nature itself. Beautiful yet dangerous. “Undine” recalls the dreamier side of 4AD, alongside Faith and the Muse and Lycia, but its bassline and guitar flourishes also make ethereal wave’s goth and post-punk origins audible. How conscious are you of that connection when writing, and what does the bass allow you to do beneath such expansive arrangements? Faded Pulse: The bassline for Undine was heavily inspired by the bassline in Slowdive’s “Ballad of Sister Sue.” I knew I wanted this waltzy song where the bass carried much of the song’s sway. To me, the bass here is the most important; it just wouldn’t sound the same with a synth bass. It really gives the song that romantic rhythm I feel it needed. The words to “Undine” address the water-born figure directly, questioning her lover’s constancy and encouraging her to voice her feelings. Whose voice did you imagine addressing her, and what did you want your interpretation to reveal about her beyond the familiar tragedy? Faded Pulse: With Undine, I knew I really wanted to do a melancholic song about a siren, where the song itself is almost like a lament, where it feels like a spell is being cast onto the listener. The voice that carries the song is part third-person narrator and part Undine’s voice. The Chorus is nonsensical and is a made-up language, but it is Undine casting her spell, hoping and praying to keep Huldbrand’s love. The third-person voice beckons Undine to own her sadness and heartbreak to sing what’s in her heart and drown in her tears, tragically ending the knight’s life, but also having the strength to embrace her own emotions of love and betrayal. “Will Thy Heart Be True?” has the feel of an ethereal folk ballad, with its knight, waiting maiden, and tests of courage. Which Arthurian or medieval texts informed the song, and what does the question of remaining true mean to you personally? Faded Pulse: I think the concept of knight and maiden came to me through William Morris’s poem “Two Red Roses Across the Moon.” Although I’ve been a fan of Morris for a few years, I first heard of it when I visited the American Arts and Crafts Museum and saw a mural depicting the maiden from the poem waiting for her knight, who was off at war. Although I love the stereotypical depiction of the medieval romance trope, the song really isn’t solely about that. It is about staying strong during dark times and finding the courage to go on, which I feel is extremely relevant. Now, the question “Will Thy Heart be True?” is really asking, “Do you have the strength to keep fighting the good fight?” even when it seems hopeless. Your influences include Romantic literature, medieval poetry, and Victorian fairy tales. Which writers have most shaped your imagination—Keats, Christina Rossetti, William Morris, or perhaps someone less immediately expected? Could you take us through one passage or story that found its way into Elysia? Faded Pulse: One of my biggest influences was Alfred Lord Tennyson’s Idylls of the King, a book I thrifted in an antique shop. It features a poetic retelling of Arthurian legends, and although none of its stories made it into Elysia, I knew I wanted Elysia to evoke the feeling of magic, mystery, and romance that the book gave me. Poems like Coleridge’s Christabel and Keats’s La Belle Dame sans Merci were hugely influential as well. Keats’s story of the Faery woman leading the gullible knight astray was definitely an inspo for Summerland. Your art-history background brings the Pre-Raphaelites, Art Nouveau, and the Arts and Crafts movement into the album’s conception. Is there a particular work by an artist such as Burne-Jones, Waterhouse, or Mucha that you could place beside one of these songs and explain the connection? Faded Pulse: Rather than a single painting, artwork, or artist, Elysia sounds like the movements as a whole and what they were trying to achieve. To me, I want people to look at any art from any of those movements and instantly think of a song from Elysia. But if I had to choose an image to associate with the album, I would choose Waterhouse’s Ophelia, as it was one of the few paintings that made me think, “I want to make music that emulates how this painting feels.” Your photographs feature flowing robes, a circlet, a sword, woodland, and Gothic architecture. Which historical garments, designers, films, or figures inform your sense of dress, and how much of that appearance comes from making or adapting things yourself? Faded Pulse: A lot of Elysia’s costumes are based on a combination of different things. For me, it was studying fashion history throughout the Middle Ages, a lot of the Medieval revival clothing coming out of the goth scene in the 90s, and of course, fantasy films like The Lord of the Rings (Particularly the elves). Photographs of Lisa Hammer and Monica Richards in the 90s and 00s were also influential on me. To me, Lisa is a modern Pre-Raphaelite fashion icon, and I definitely wanted to emulate that for Elysia. A lot of the wardrobe for the photos was thrifted or modified to achieve that vibe. What do you think made ethereal wave such a natural home for medieval romance, folklore, and mystery? Within your own music, what do those older forms of imagination allow you to say about love, longing, or belonging in the present? Faded Pulse: I think there’s something very classic about medieval folklore and stories. They feel very timeless with their usage of romance, bravery, and fighting for something you think is worth fighting for. They capture what it means to be human and to be alive. I think Medieval and Ethereal are so drawn to each other because they both have a sense of whimsy and otherworldliness. I think this element of fantasy is so unique to Ethereal outside of the other core genres of the gothic scene. With ethereal, I can weave stories and ambiance that fully immerse the listener into the world I want to create, and I think that’s why fairytales and ethereal go so well together; it’s a perfect mesh of storytelling and sonic immersion. An enduring part of the Gothic imagination is its embrace of mystery and the wonders of nature. Do you feel that connection is more important than ever in this age of AI, and what role can music play in keeping that sense of wonder alive? Faded Pulse: I think music is more important now than ever in the age of AI. It requires you to engage no matter what, to let go, sit down, and spend your time listening, to feel something. I think music is intrinsically human, and I feel that when people go out to clubs or venues for shows and connect with those around them, it really helps them disconnect from the haze of being online all the time and brings them into the present. There is something magical about watching people perform and bring something out of you. That is something that AI could never replace. If you could present Elysia in a setting entirely of your choosing, what would a Faded Pulse performance look and feel like? How would the space, clothing, and instrumentation help bring listeners into these songs, and what would you want them to feel when they stepped outside again? Faded Pulse: I think two of my dream performance locations would be a medieval ruin or within the Met Cloisters Museum in New York. I feel like being surrounded by actual medieval art and architecture would really set the ambiance. One thing I’ve heard of is that bands in the 90s would have incense burning on stage. I don’t know how true that is, and of course, venues would never allow that now, but I think something like frankincense or sandalwood would be my chosen scent, and I feel like playing with multiple senses would really elevate the performance. For dress, I think it would be cool to have a lot of the new-agey medieval revival looks from the nineties that were popular in the scene, and, of course, I would encourage everyone to participate in dressing up if they so choose. For me, I want the audience to feel like they entered another realm, dreamy and untethered, and when they leave, feeling like they had a spiritual awakening.§ For all its mythic tales of knights, faeries, and enchanted waters, Elysia is an album that keeps returning to the ordinary work of being present: listening closely, making something, finding courage, and spending time with other people. Johnson’s ideal audience might gather in velvet beneath medieval arches, but the invitation extends well beyond that imagined evening. There is room for wonder in a borrowed book, a local show, or an afternoon among the trees, and Faded Pulse offers plenty of reasons to make room for it. Faded Pulse’s Elysia is out now. Listen to the album below and order here. items.body: 2026.09.23 デビュー20周年を迎え、ベートーヴェンのチェロ・ソナタ全5曲に挑む新倉瞳さん。なぜ今、ベートーヴェンなのか？ 7歳でチェロと出会ったきっかけから、音楽家として大切にしていること、憧れの音楽家、新しいジャンルへの挑戦まで……新倉さんの音楽人生と「今」が見えてくる50の質問を前後編でお届けします。 ONTOMO編集部 東京・神楽坂にある音楽之友社を拠点に、Webマガジン「ONTOMO」の企画・取材・編集をしています。「音楽っていいなぁ、を毎日に。」を掲げ、やさしく・ふかく・おもしろ... 詳しく見る デビュー20周年の節目にベートーヴェンのチェロ・ソナタ全曲に挑む 1. デビュー20周年おめでとうございます！ 20年前の自分に、今の新倉さんから一言かけるとしたら、何と言いますか？ 新倉 「安心していいよ」と言いたいです。自分が思っている自分と、他人から見える自分には、どうしても差があります。100人の人がいたら、100通りの自分の見え方があると思うんです。 20年前は「こうでなければいけない」とすごく気にしていました。でも今は、みんなが思ってくださった自分が自分でしかないと思えるようになりました。自分が思っていることを、意外とちゃんと見てくださっている方々もいらっしゃるので、そういったところでリラックスして、安心して楽しんでいればいいよ、と言いたいですね。 新倉瞳（にいくら・ひとみ） 桐朋学園大学音楽学部を首席で卒業し、皇居桃華楽堂新人演奏会に出演して御前演奏を行う。その後スイスに渡り、バーゼル音楽院ソリストコース・教職課程の両修士課程を最高点で修了。これまでに毛利伯郎、堤剛、トーマス・デメンガ、マーティン・ツェラー（バロック・チェロ）の各氏に師事。国内外で数多くの賞を受賞し、2017年に第18回ホテルオークラ音楽賞、2020年度に第19回齋藤秀雄メモリアル基金賞チェロ部門を受賞。桐朋学園大学在学中にEMI Music Japanより『鳥の歌』でCDデビューし、同レーベルから3枚、アールアンフィニからは『11月の夜想曲～委嘱作品集』を含む4枚のソロアルバムをリリース。ほかにも多数のアルバムを発表している。 かつてカメラータ・チューリッヒのソロ首席チェリストとして活躍し、スイスを拠点にヨーロッパや中央アジア、日本でもソリストや室内楽奏者として幅広く活動する。近年はクレズマー音楽や民族音楽にも造詣を深め、音楽祭に招かれワークショップやレクチャーコンサートも行う。カザフスタンの民俗楽器ドンブラも演奏し、2025年にはカザフスタン国営放送で日本人として異例の紹介を受けた。 使用楽器は宗次コレクションより貸与のマッテオ・ゴフリラー（1710年製）。2026年にデビュー20周年を迎えた。 2. 20周年の節目として、12月3日に俳優の南沢奈央さんの語りとともにベートーヴェンのチェロ・ソナタを舞台のように届ける演奏会「ベートーヴェンの小径」を開催されます。まず、ベートーヴェンを取り上げようと思った理由を教えてください。どんな演出になるのでしょうか？ 新倉 私はいろんなジャンルの音楽に興味を持って活動してきましたが、20周年ということで、いわゆる「ザ・クラシック」みたいなプログラムに取り組みたいという思いもありました。これまで民俗音楽にも多く取り組んできましたが、ベートーヴェンの作品も紐解いていくと、民俗音楽との関連が見えてきます。だからこそ、節目の年にベートーヴェンのチェロ・ソナタ全曲を取り上げるのは、すごくいいのではないかと思いました。 さらに、私のデビュー20周年の次の年がベートーヴェンの没後200年なので、長い期間で、お祭りみたいにできるかなと思った次第です。 演出については、当日までのお楽しみです。ただ、音楽をいわゆる舞台の主役にして、チェロ・ソナタが本編となって、語りの部分が幕間をつないでいくような感じにしたいと思っています。 3. 「ベートーヴェンの小径」では、演奏だけでなく構成・脚本・演出も手がけられます。なぜこのような舞台形式でベートーヴェンを届けたいと思われたのでしょうか？ 新倉 ベートーヴェンのチェロ・ソナタを改めて勉強して、ベートーヴェンの生きてきた背景や彼が残した言葉などいろいろなものをリサーチしていくうちに、ものすごく面白いと思ったんです。そして、演奏で伝えることが使命ではありますが、せっかくだったら物語を交えてみるのはどうかな、と思いました。 南沢奈央さんとは、以前『罪と罰』という舞台でご一緒したことがあって、そのときも音楽が物語に介入していくような演出でした。南沢さんとその後ご飯に行ったときに、彼女も今年がデビュー20周年だと知り、「じゃあ何か一緒にやれたらいいね」と言って別れたんです。 その帰り道に、もし彼女にベートーヴェンのチェロ・ソナタでご一緒していただけるんだったら、そういった物語を本当に組み込めるかもしれないと思いついて。いろんな点と点が、ピーンとつながったんです。 もうひとつの拠点、スイスで、著名な音楽家の方が演奏曲の背景をさらっとお話ししてからコンサートをするのを見て、すごく勉強になったんです。「こういうひと言があると入っていきやすいな」と。だから、演出とか脚本という言葉にするとすごくドラマティックですが、自然な流れなんじゃないかなと思っています。総合プロデュースとして、作曲家と曲の魅力や、自分が思っていることをお伝えできるきっかけになるんじゃないかなと思っています。 新倉瞳 × 南沢奈央「ベートーヴェンの小径」 4. ベートーヴェンの5曲のチェロ・ソナタの中で、今のご自身に一番近いと感じる作品はどれですか？ 新倉 今の自分に一番近いと感じるのは、もしかしたら3番かもしれません。 私は、そのときに取り組んでいる曲が一番大事だと思うタイプ。でも、ベートーヴェンの5曲のソナタをそれぞれ見ていくと、1番と2番はベートーヴェン自身がピアノを弾いていたこともあって、ピアノが主役で、チェロはオブリガートのような役割なんですね。 それに対して第3番は、ベートーヴェンがいわゆるチェロ・ソナタとして舞台に乗せることを意識して作っているので、第1番、第2番とは全然違うんです。第4番、第5番になると、さらに即興的な要素も入ってきます。 そう考えると、自分が演奏家として人前に出るという意味では、第3番が一つのきっかけのような存在なのかなと思います。ロマンティックな部分もすごくあって、ロマン派への入り口にもなっていますし。 ただ、ベートーヴェン自身がソナタに対していろいろなアプローチをしていったように、私自身も変化していくと思うんです。だから、数年後には「やっぱり第5番かな」と言っているかもしれません。 初めてチェロを弾いたときに「もっといい音を出したい」と思った 5. チェロを始めたきっかけを教えてください。 新倉 もともと母がピアニストで、お腹の中にいるときからピアノを聴いていました。自然ななりゆきで母からピアノを教わっていたんですが、普段は優しい母なのに、ピアノの前では急に角がはえてきて（笑）。それで、だんだんピアノが怖くなってしまいました。 当時、父の仕事の関係でドイツに住んでいたこともあって、音楽がいろんな方とのコミュニケーションのツールになるということは、よく感じていました。音楽自体はもちろん大好きだったけど、ピアノを弾くことが怖くなってしまった私を見かねて、7歳くらいのときに母がドイツのトーンハレというライン川のほとりにある劇場に、よくコンサートに連れて行ってくれました。 母は、ピアノでなくてもハープやフルートといった女性が構えて美しい楽器を趣味でいいから演奏してくれたらといいなと思っていたらしいんです。でも、その頃オーケストラや室内楽を聴いて、「チェロって、すごく支えているのに主役にもなれるし、いろんな面があって、何より音色がきれいで、いい楽器だな」と思って、母に「あれがやりたい」と言ったんです。 そのとき母は、「足を開く楽器を選んだ！」と思ってびっくりしたらしいんですけど、8歳の誕生日にチェロがやってきました。 7歳にしてチェロに魅了されたという新倉さん 6. 初めてチェロを弾いたとき、どんな印象を持ちましたか？ 新倉 もちろん、体に当たって音が響くことには「わー」と感動しました。 でも、まだ小さかったのでフルサイズではなくて1/2サイズの子ども用のチェロだったんです。大人の演奏で聴いていたよりも、「あれ、なんか音があんまりよくない？」と思って。「もっといい音を出したい」と思いました。思っている音色じゃない、というのはすごく覚えています。当時から早くフルサイズになりたいと思っていました。 7. 子どもの頃、一番好きだったチェロの曲は何ですか？ 新倉 今思うと、ヴィヴァルディのチェロ・ソナタ第5番ですね。 わりと小さいときに取り組んだ曲だったんです。ヴィヴァルディの《四季》がすごく好きだったので、「チェロでもヴィヴァルディが弾けるんだ！」というところで、子どもの頃から好きでした。チェロを始めて1、2年後、わりと早い段階で取り組んでいました。 ヴィヴァルディ：チェロ・ソナタ第5番第1楽章 8. 「音楽家になろう」と決めたのは、いつ頃でしたか？ 新倉 中学生のときです。ピアノがちょっと怖くなって以降、チェロに関してはものすごく自由に、練習したいときに練習して、ほかの習い事も並行していました。クラシックバレエ、水泳、テニス、塾など、いろいろさせてもらっていたんです。 中学生のときには、絵描きや美術の道に進むことにも憧れがあって、どちらにしても芸術なんですけれども、少し悩んでいました。そんなときに、パブロ・カザルスの国連でのスピーチで、「わたしの故郷カタルーニャの鳥はピース、ピースと鳴くのです」とおっしゃっているのを聞いて、「どうして人間は争っているんだ」と思ったんです。 それはいまだに消えないテーマなんですけど、「音楽がそういった平和にちゃんと響くことができるんだ」と思って、絶対に音楽家になろうと思いました。 クレズマー音楽との出会いによって「優等生」から解放 9. 音楽家になっていなかったら、何になりたかったですか？ 新倉 絵描きに憧れがありました。薄い色を重ねる水彩画は苦手で、はっきりとした、わりとおどろおどろしい絵を描いていました（笑）。 10. これまでの音楽人生で、ご自身が大きく変わったと感じた出来事は？ 新倉 いまだに真面目気質ではあるんですけれども、今はだいぶ「不真面目になること」に、いい意味で慣れるようになったなと思っています。 大学生のときにデビューして、優等生でいないといけないという時期もありましたが、スイスで東ヨーロッパのクレズマー音楽に出会って、プロもアマチュアもいるバンドに参加するようになったんです。そこで、「優等生である必要ないな」と思って。音楽が好きで集まって、みんなで弾いている気持ちって、すごく大事だなと思うようになりました。 そこからすごく気持ちが落ち着いて、そうすると、キャリアもなぜか追いついてきたというか。クレズマー音楽に出会って、自分が「優等生でいなくちゃいけない」という意識がなくなったときに、すごく解放されたなと思います。 クレズマー音楽も収録したアルバム『魂柱と鞴』 11. もしチェロ以外の楽器をマスターできるとしたら、何を選びますか？ 新倉 実は2つあって、1つは昔から打楽器が大好きなんです。リズムってやっぱりすごいなというイメージがあります。今も趣味でサンバヘギというサンバの太鼓を叩いています。実は音楽之友社さんの前からスタートする神楽坂のパレードで、何回か叩いたことがあります。 あとは歌ですね。自分の声が楽器というのは憧れがあります。それができないから、チェロで歌を表現している部分があるのかなと思います。 歌は自分が楽器だから、それがダイレクトに伝わると思うんです。でも、それって生まれ持ったものもあると思うので、私は次はもっとカラオケでバリバリ歌える声質で生まれてきたいなと思います。 2025年「化け猫フェスティバル」より 編集部員にとっておなじみの会社周辺の光景に新倉さんが打楽器を演奏する姿が……！ 動画は新倉瞳さんのInstagramで！ 大切にしているのは「一音入魂」 12. 新倉さんにとって、チェロの一番好きなところはどこですか？ 新倉 歌を表現できるところです！ 13. 一番の思い出の曲は？ 新倉 エルガーのチェロ協奏曲です。取り組んでいた中学生のときに、祖父が亡くなったんです。私にとって初めての大好きな人の旅立ちだったので、人間の魂というものが音に乗るという経験を初めてしました。叫びきれない思いをチェロに乗せて叫べた、そういった経験ができました。 14. 生涯でチェロ協奏曲を1曲しか弾けないとしたら、どの作品を選びますか？ 新倉 これもエルガーのチェロ協奏曲です。高校受験のときにも取り組みましたが、エルガーはとても深みがあるので、大人になってから取り組むというイメージがあったんですけれど、ドロドロした絵を描くタイプだったからこそ、その深い音楽にシンパシーを感じていたのかもしれません。 新倉さんによるエルガー：チェロ協奏曲 15. 演奏するときに、一番大切にしていることは何ですか？ 新倉 「一音入魂」です。一音一音、そこに何か意味がある音を出したいと思っています。 なんとなく音符を追うのではなく、「作曲家はどうしてこの音を残して、私はどのようにそれを汲み取ったらよいのだろう」とすり合わせて、音に魂を込めたいなと思っています。 16. 練習中など壁にぶつかったときはどうやって乗り越えますか？ 新倉 結局、ひたすら納得いくまで練習するしかないなと思います。私は悩みをそのままにしておけないタイプなので、悩みきることのほうが気持ちいいんです。ぶつかっていきますね。 練習したくない気分のときは、あまり悩まないで、やめて、ご飯を食べに行くなど気分転換して、また向き合います。 本番前のルーティンはなし！ 17. 本番前は緊張するタイプですか？ 新倉 準備が整っていると、あまりしないかな。もうやるしかないと思っているから。逆に、練習中のほうが「これ、間違えたらどうしよう」と緊張することもあります。そういうことを練習中に考えて、本番前は「ここまでやったから、もう大丈夫だろう」と思って挑みます。 18. 本番前に必ずすること、ルーティンはありますか？ 新倉 あまり決めないほうがいいと思っています。日本のコンサートホールのように楽屋がきちんとある環境ばかりではなく、海外の教会で寒い日にいきなり弾かなければならないこともある。そうすると、ルーティンを決めていて、それができなかったときに焦ってしまうんじゃないかなと思うんです。 なので、練習を始めるときは曲をパッと弾いて、弾けなかったところが自分のウィークポイントだと思うようにしています。 19. 「今日はいい演奏ができた」と感じるのは、どんなときですか？ 新倉 結局、自分にはどうしても厳しくなってしまうので、共演者やお客さまがいい顔、いい表情をしていたら「よかったのかな」と思えます。自分基準ではあまり判断できないので、ほかの人がいい顔をしているかどうかで「よかったのかな」と思えます。 ちなみにスタイルキープの秘訣は「服のサイズを変えないこと」だそう！ 20. 今、一番弾いていて楽しい作曲家は誰ですか？ 新倉 今はベートーヴェンです。常に変わっているんですが、今はベートーヴェンに改めて取り組んでいて、新しい発見がたくさんあります。 以前に聴いたときとは、やっぱり自分が変わっている。特にベートーヴェンは、私が幼少期に聴いてきた演奏は、どちらかというとロマンティックな演奏が多かったんです。 ベートーヴェンのチェロ・ソナタ1番、2番は、チェロがオブリガート的な役目だと先ほどお話ししましたが、それでもチェロがリッチに演奏されることが今まですごく多かった。 でも、今改めて勉強し直してみると、ピアノとチェロの対話が面白いんです。例えば、チェロから始まるフレーズだと思って弾いていた部分が、改めて見るとピアノから呼応する形で出てきているんだな、と。そう考えると、「もっとさらっと弾いてよかったんだな」と思ったり。自分なりの解釈がはっきりしてきたというのが、楽しいです。 21. これまでに「この人の音楽はすごい！」と衝撃を受けた音楽家はいますか？ 新倉 1人ではないんですが、あえて1人選ばせていただくなら、堤剛先生です。堤先生の音って、どの曲を聴いてもわかるんです。 私とは違う解釈で演奏されていても、ショパンやリヒャルト・シュトラウスのチェロ・ソナタ、ドヴォルザークの協奏曲、バッハなど、先生の説得力のある音が今でも耳に残っています。音色だけでなく、生徒としてではなく、常に一人の芸術家として接してくださったことも大きいです。 私が自分に自信をなくしていたときには「あなたの実力でここまで来ている」と背中を押してくださったり、クレズマー音楽など新しいことにも「素晴らしいですね」と耳を傾けてくださったり。学生時代には、クラシックではない民族音楽のCDをプレゼントしてくださったこともありました。 そういう意味でも、堤先生は私にとって特別な存在です。 ジャンルが違うと思いすぎずに新しい出会いを楽しむ 22. 今後一緒に演奏してみたい音楽家を一人挙げるとしたら、誰ですか？ 新倉 まだ存じ上げていない方との出会いがある気がしているので、そういう方との出会いを楽しみにしたいです。今この時点で、あえて1人挙げるとしたら、ダニエル・ゼペックさんです。 バーゼルに留学中に室内楽の授業を受けたのですが、一緒に演奏すると学べることがあると思います。ゼペックさんのベートーヴェンの音楽にも感銘を受けたので、一緒に室内楽を弾いてみたいです。 ダニエル・ゼペックによるベートーヴェン：ピアノ三重奏曲 23. ジャンルを越えた活動にも取り組まれていますが、新しい音楽に出会うときに大切にしていることは何ですか？ 新倉 結局、あまり「ジャンルが違う」と考えすぎないことだと思っています。自分が知らないことは、同じジャンルの中にもまだまだありますから。 新しい音楽に惹かれるときも、音楽そのものというより、「なぜこの魅力的な人は、この音楽を取り入れているんだろう」というところから興味を持つことが多いですね。 クレズマーなど東ヨーロッパの音楽に没頭していったのも、プロとアマチュアが一緒に演奏するバンドに入ったことがきっかけでした。音楽の響きはもちろんですが、そういう人たちに感動していることが多いんだと思います。 24. 今、音楽家として一番知りたいこと、探求したいことは何ですか？ 新倉 今回ベートーヴェンに取り組むことで、ベートーヴェンの知られざる一面をたくさん発見できました。なので、今回の12月3日の公演でも、きっと皆さまも「あ、そうなんだ」というところが見つかると思います。「そういう曲を書いていたんだ」とか、「そういう一面があるんだ」と。そういった意味で、残された曲に関しては、書かれた背景や作曲家の人となりを探求したいと思います。 うつむくベートーヴェンを気にかけてあげる新倉さん 25. これから、どんな音楽家になっていきたいですか？ 新倉 私は有名な国際コンクールに入賞しているわけでもないのですが、それでも第一線の皆さんと一緒に音を出させていただく機会に恵まれてきました。 なので、これからの若い方々が何か挫折したときに「あ、こういう音楽家もいた」と思っていただけるような、何か一つの例になれたらいいのかなと思っています。 いろいろなキャリアや肩書きがなくても、「自分なりの道があるよ」と思っていただける存在になりたいなと思っているので、それをキープ・ゴーイングでいきたいです。 新倉瞳に50の質問！〈後編〉新倉瞳の人となりは9月30日公開予定！ ポッドキャストの視聴はこちら 新倉瞳さんの出演情報 新倉瞳 × 南沢奈央 ベートーヴェンの小径 日時： 2026年12月3日（木）19：00開演 会場： サントリーホール ブルーローズ 曲目： 語りとともに綴るベートーヴェンの世界 ベートーヴェン／チェロ・ソナタ全曲 構成・脚本・演出： 新倉 瞳 出演： 新倉瞳（チェロ）、南沢奈央（語り）、横山瑠佳（ピアノ） スペシャルゲスト： 大萩 康司（ギター）、佐藤 芳明（アコーディオン）、大渕 愛子（フィドル）、渡辺 庸介（パーカッション） 詳しくはこちら

items.album: ネットの荒らし
items.excerpt: ■はじめに・この記事は、荒らし行為（ネット上で場を乱す、挑発する、中傷する、妨害する行為）とそれを行う人について、公的資料、学術研究、法律解説、報道を集めて整理したものです。・「荒らし」「炎上」「誹謗中傷」は重なる部分もありますが、別の概念です。混ぜて語ると誤解のもとなので、順に分けて書きます。・法律部分は一般的な情報であり、個別の案件の法的助言ではありません。実際に被害に遭った場合は、弁護士や公的窓口へ相談してください。・調査結果の中には古いものや、原典を確認できていない二次情報もあります。その場合は本文中で断っています。続きをみる

items.body: As you are likely well aware, this week marks the 100th anniversary of John Coltrane's birth and writers and friends of the Free Jazz Blog were asked to contribute their personal thoughts on his music and influence. The parameters for the contributions were loose, only that it should be something personal and if it so happened that an album appeared more than once, that was fine, as what it meant to the writer was surely different. We ended up with our biggest feature ever! For the next two weeks we will be featuring reflections, reviews, and anecdotes about Coltrane and his groundbreaking music. We begin today an introduction from Sammy Stein. Enjoy! Paul Acquaro John Coltrane. Src: wikipedia By Sammy Stein FJC is celebrating John Coltrane’s 100 th year. For anyone unfamiliar with his music, the following offers a brief overview of why Coltrane is ranked amongst the greatest of musicians. Through his approach, style, delivery, and unmistakable sound, Coltrane powered through the door that Ornette Coleman and others had left ajar, revealing jazz’s powerful, emotive, and transformational heart. Nothing post-Coltrane is untouched by his influence. His was not a deliberate subversion of traditional jazz, but an uncalculated stream of events, personal, spiritual, and historical, that converged in a confluence that formed his music. Coltrane’s mother bought him a saxophone when he was sixteen, and he was influenced by players including Illinois Jacquet. His grandparents were ordained ministers, his parents met through the church, and Coltrane grew up influenced by religion. He chose a different path – that of music and was not discouraged by family, yet later in his life, it was God who helped him save his music and career. Without his spiritual reawakening, Coltrane’s career may have faded. Early on, he was supported by musicians who recognised his prodigious talent. However, he became addicted to drugs and would arrive for gigs unshaven and in smelly, wrinkled clothes. He might fall asleep on stage. Miles Davis fired him, and Dizzy Gillespie didn’t follow suit only because of their friendship and his respect for Coltrane’s talent. At the nadir of his life, Coltrane reached out to God. He described a revelation he had when God spoke to him, and he set about composing exquisite music, praising God and teaching his followers. He said, “My goal is to live the truly religious life and express it through my music. If you can live it, there’s no problem about the music, because it’s part of the whole thing.” Coltrane’s first wife, Naima, was central to his early spiritual journey. A practicing Muslim, she helped him understand God’s presence in their lives. With her support, he overcame addiction within a year. His second wife, Alice, became his spiritual partner and musical collaborator. A pianist and harpist, she understood Coltrane’s desire to contribute to a greater purpose through music. Some of Coltrane’s music has an intangible quality. He understood the spiritual and temporal worlds, and his music fused the two, expressing deep spiritual inquiry alongside the mortal complexities of personality. Jazz became a place where the human condition could be expressed with unflinching honesty and transcendent beauty. Coltrane was playing at a time when conditions were ripe for rebellion and change, and he was profoundly affected by events of his time, especially the civil rights movement, initially siding with Malcolm X before aligning with Martin Luther King Jr’s belief in peaceful but persistent protest. He performed eight benefit concerts to support Martin Luther King Jr’s cause. His music channeled anger at racism and discrimination, despair at humanity’s darkness, and the beauty of praise and worship. He had faced the demons of addiction and won, and his music reflected beauty, was personal yet spoke to millions. The murder of four African American girls in the KKK bombing in Birmingham, Alabama, in 1963 profoundly affected Coltrane. Two months after the event, he took McCoy Tyner, Jimmy Garrison, and Elvin Jones into Rudy Van Gelder's studio and recorded ‘Alabama’, later released on the album Live At Birdland (Impulse 1964). As discontent rose, Coltrane’s modal technique challenged preconceived ideas about traditional jazz. Under his and other musicians’ tenure, jazz, ever the mirror of society, became more dissonant and unruly. Coltrane’s music is as relevant today as it was in the 1960s. The messages are clearly and profoundly expressed and cut to the core impulses of humanity. Because of his uncloaked humanity, listening to Coltrane feels as emergent and alive for someone encountering the music today as it did to listeners forty years, or ten years ago. Coltrane’s near-mythical status was helped by the Blue Note label, which signed Coltrane and other players, seen as risky at the time, and some iconic images, notably photographs by Francis Wolff, a skilled photographer and executive of Blue Note. Of over 33,000 pictures Wolff took (probably more), his images of John Coltrane in moments of intense concentration or creativity seem to capture the musician's essence. One of Coltrane’s gifts was his ability to perform as a soloist or as part of an ensemble. Pieces like Davis’s’ ‘Milestones’ with ‘Cannonball’ Adderley (alto sax) and Coltrane (tenor sax) responding to Davis’s trumpet with twists and turns within the original mode laid a template for modal playing (try also Coltrane's’ Spiral’ and ‘Naima’ from Giant Steps (Atlantic 1959)). Modal jazz led away from traditional jazz and toward free jazz. Free playing was where Coltrane was headed. In the 1960s, some journalists described early free jazz as a poison to jazz, and Downbeat critics described Coltrane and Dolphy’s playing as ‘nihilistic exercises’ and ‘anti-jazz.’ Miles Davis found free jazz difficult to embrace initially. However, a few years later Davis, like Coltrane and others, found free jazz liberating. Coltrane, like many free-playing musicians, connected the evolution of the music with a deepening of self-realization and the strengthening and expression of their beliefs. Alongside fellow musicians Yusef Lateef, Sonny Rollins, and others, Coltrane pursued musical mastery and self-realization. In his suite A Love Supreme (Impulse, 1965), Coltrane expressed his love and awe of God, and the final movement is based on a devotional poem he wrote. He studied different religions and philosophies, including the Indian philosophy of Jiddu Krishnamurti, which he was introduced to by Bill Evans. Coltrane perhaps expressed his love for God most during his free playing. His tracks ‘Love’ and ‘The Father, And The Son And the Holy Ghost’ on Meditations (Impulse 1965), albums Ascension (Impulse 1966), Om (Impulse, recorded 1965, released 1966), and ‘Peace on Earth’ from Infinity (Impulse, recorded 1966, released 1972), reflect his beliefs. Coltrane used the ferocity of his playing and complex techniques as a way of worship. He said he created music for God and others and wanted to be the opposing force to evil. Even those unaware of his driving beliefs find something special, untouchable, and unique in his music. Coltrane, Art Blakey, Yusef Lateef, and other musicians became part of the Ahmadiyya sect of Islam, which forbids the intake of drugs and alcohol. Coltrane said, "My music is the spiritual expression of what I am - my faith, my knowledge, my being. When you begin to see the possibilities of music, you desire to do something really good for people, to help humanity free itself from its hang-ups…I want to speak to their souls.” Some found Coltrane’s later music, with its contradictions and unresolved transitions, less pure than his earlier recordings, but for many, they remain some of the best work produced by any jazz musician. Two weeks before his death, Coltrane discussed opening a music venue without alcohol as he realized this had masked his creativity. After Coltrane died in 1967, aged just forty, Alice kept pushing musical boundaries, and her music took on a profoundly spiritual element. She collaborated with Ornette Coleman, Pharoah Sanders, and many others, and her music traversed from blues-infused melodies to unfathomable sonic journeys, but it was beautiful, and her talent won armies of devotees, so, partly through Alice, Coltrane’s legacy remained. Also through his sons. John Jr, Ravi, and Oranyan. Oranyan started playing jazz with his brothers but has gone into trance and electronic music production. John Jr was a promising bassist but was killed in a car accident when he was 17, and Ravi is a jazz musician. Alice’s grandnephew, Steven Ellison, AKA Flying Lotus, is a record label owner, producer, rapper, and DJ. Many of his recordings feature jazz samples. Coltrane’s music and persona continue to influence music and musicians. From those who followed directly, including Pharoah Sanders, Lonnie Liston, Sun Ra, Don Cherry, and John McLaughlin, to nearly every jazz musician today. In 2016,’ Alabama’ was included in John DeJohnette's 2016 album In Movement (ECM), and on this recording, sons of the original artists, including saxophonist Ravi Coltrane (son of Coltrane) and bassist Matthew Garrison (son of bassist Jimmy Garrison), played. Coltrane’s music has been sampled on recordings by hip hop artists, younger jazz musicians, and many others. FJC is celebrating the fact that Coltrane left his influence, and there are some great pieces following this introduction. It is impossible to adequately record the influence of John Coltrane on the music that followed, but we can try. As a jazz musician recently said to me, ‘Don’t worry, just stick on some ‘Trane.” Perhaps more than any other jazz musician, John Coltrane showed there is a way to play from the heart without constraints. When you can do that, you allow your true spirit to reveal itself. Like ‘Trane. Email This BlogThis! Share to X Share to Facebook

items.body: Pendulum is a singular piano trio featuring French pianist Benoît Delbecq with Danish double bass player Jonas Westergaard and drummer Peter Bruun (both Westergaard and Bruun have collaborated before with fellow Danish pianist Søren Kjærgaard). Bruun initiated this trio in 2024 as part of his ambitious research project exploring new approaches to musical time (Multitemporal movement and embodiment through Rhythmic Design at The Danish National Academy of Music). The Pendulum trio investigates all aspects of this classic format, including the most basic sensibilities of space and time, avoiding rigid structures, allowing instead for balance, elegance and fluidity. It challenges us to listen to its music as resonant arcs or shared fields of presence rather than defined by linear time, and explores new ways to transform free improvisation gravity into groove. Delbeq suggested that the trio will play with the presence of physical pendulums on stage, symbolizing the elasticity of time and giving a sense of pulse. These oscillating bodies guide the subtle, cyclical shifts in the music, which, paradoxically, feels familiar: music that sways and breathes, while finding rhythm in the inevitability of motion. The trio releases its eight-volume EP series, Arcs , nearly three hours of music, in a monthly release cycle that began in May and will conclude in December 2026. These Arcs offer Pendulum’s idiosyncratic, enigmatic, lyrical universe, in which metric relations, shifting balances, and elastic phrasing are woven together in a kaleidoscopic manner. Each volume swings on its own terms, with no intention to offer a linear narrative, and uses distinct compositional fragments, notated and graphic scores. But the whole project accumulates into an open body of work that allows us to feel how time bends, breathes, and searches for an elusive balance. The Pendulum trio invites listeners to form their own path through the eight volumes and discover different insights and relations in their own time. Arc No. 1 Pendulum describes this volume: “Time leans before it moves. Motion unfolds patiently, stretching and rebounding with quiet elasticity. What propels the arc is not force but attentiveness, which allows duration to bend and return without breaking. Each swing carries clarity and restraint, revealing time as something more shaped than measured”. The trio suggests sparse, deep listening, labyrinthine architectures with patient and subtle, cyclical-rhythmic shifts, best captured in the aptly titled, 17-minute minimalist “Exercice Elastique”, that patiently gravitates into a most delicate, vulnerable, quite irreverent groove. Arc No. 2 “Afterwards appears before it is recognized. Movement writes itself into space, leaving subtle traces that guide listening rather than direction. Rhythms form paths, both adaptable and responsive, where perception stretches between memory and anticipation. The arc remains fluid, shaped by change rather than arrival”. Pendulum sketches an almost abstract, empty map, from which it begins to imagine possible contours and paths, and how to find its inner, spatial logic, and its subtle rhythmic shifts, finally realized on “Plasticity”. Arc No. 3 “Movement turns inward. Each gesture is weighted, deliberate, and reduced to necessity. Time thickens as motion slows, inviting attention to settle inside the smallest shifts. The arc transforms discreetly, as intensity is held beneath restraint. Balance is discovered through presence, not display”. The 31-minute “Buto” corresponds with the hyper-slow and hyper-controlled motion of the Japanese avant-dance theatre, Butō (舞踏), that resists and fixated conception of time. Pendulum’s fragile balance was realized through an austere, cryptic, and often almost silent presence that keeps triggering our imagination, and not by technical display or mastery. Arc No. 4 “Wooden time moves with grain and resistance. Motion creaks, sways, and negotiates its own structure. Oscillation becomes tactile, shaped by friction and patience. The arc holds multiple possibilities at once, allowing form and freedom to coexist without resolution. The rings of time are both counted and counting”. The trio focuses on its essence, the ever-negotiated arcs that blur the distinction between form and freedom, and question our conception of linear time, turning it into a spiritual riddle, a kōan. Arc No. 5 “A phase shifts nearly unnoticed. Motion lightens, stepping carefully through softened contours. Layers thin and overlap, revealing phrasing where gestures begin and fade. The arc listens closely to its own balance, finding meaning in nuance rather than emphasis. The push and pull are their own reason for being”. Pendulum refines its fragile, nuanced equilibrium with melodic threads that patiently, hesitantly flirt with familiar, playful, and resonant piano trio dynamics. Arc No. 6 (to be released on October 10) “Momenta accumulate through return. Motion becomes practiced, framed by shared gravity and memory. Energy circulates without urgency, shaped by repetition and transformation. The past is present and future at once”. A further, urgent, cyclical rhythmic refinement is offered, faithfully captured in the short pieces “Arc” and “Dance”, shaped by nuanced repetitions and transformations. Arc No. 7 (to be released on November 9) “Time folds into itself. Multiple cycles coexist, asymmetrical yet connected. Movement breathes across layered durations, allowing contradiction to remain unresolved. The arc sustains density without weight, continuity without uniformity. Listening is wide enough to hold all the all of it”. Pendulum’s music plays a touch-and-go game in its own fragmented musical continuum, sustaining density without weight, continuity without uniformity, but with more structural focus. Arc No. 8 (to be released on December 9) “Strange tools reveal their logic through use. Motion disperses, leaving resonance rather than momentum. What remains feels everywhere at once, absorbed into space and attention. The arc settles without closing, as stillness carries the last trace of movement forward. It is the beginning of the end and the end of the beginning”. The concluding volume is not an end to this fascinating journey but a sort of beginning. The Pendulum trio already inhabited its own elastic conception of time, as the devoted listeners to this journey, and has established its idiosyncratic language. But Pendulum’s music tells us something deeper about life and the inevitable changes we experience throughout life. This trio asks us to adapt our time sensibility to its subtle transformations, fully embrace and be deeply attuned to our own ubiquitous cyclical and oscillating arcs, as we move forward, attempting to maintain an elusive balance. <a href="https://ilkmusiccph.bandcamp.com/album/opening-arcs-arc-no-1">Opening Arcs: Arc No. 1 by Pendulum (Benoit Delbecq, Jonas Westergaard, Peter Bruun)</a > <a href="https://ilkmusiccph.bandcamp.com/album/opening-arcs-arc-no-2">Opening Arcs: Arc no. 2 by Pendulum (Benoit Delbecq, Jonas Westergaard, Peter Bruun)</a > <a href="https://ilkmusiccph.bandcamp.com/album/pendulum-opening-arcs-arc-no-3">Pendulum – Opening Arcs: Arc no. 3 by Pendulum (Benoît Delbecq, Jonas Westergaard, Peter Bruun)</a > <a href="https://ilkmusiccph.bandcamp.com/album/pendulum-opening-arcs-arc-no-4">Pendulum – Opening Arcs: Arc no. 4 by Pendulum (Benoît Delbecq, Jonas Westergaard, Peter Bruun)</a > <a href="https://ilkmusiccph.bandcamp.com/album/opening-arcs-arc-no-5">Opening Arcs: Arc no. 5 by ILK</a > Email This BlogThis! items.body:
Berlin got a taste of Korean indie rock as CATCH THE YOUNG took over Säälchen for the opening night of K-INDIE ON FESTIVAL – No Borders, Just RocK! on 19 September.

The five-piece band — NAMHYUN, KIHOON, SANI, JUNYONG, and JUNGMO — delivered a 13-song set for the German crowd, bringing their self-described “YOUTH-POP ROCK” sound to the fourth edition of the festival.

Hosted by the Korean Cultural Center in Germany, K-INDIE ON FESTIVAL has been introducing German audiences to Korean music beyond K-pop since 2023. This edition kicked off at Säälchen before continuing for its second day at Holzmarkt.

View this post on Instagram

A post shared by CATCH THE YOUNG(캐치더영) (@catch_theyoung)

For CATCH THE YOUNG, their Berlin appearance was all about meeting the crowd at full force. “The incredible passion and energy from the Berlin audience really pushed us to give it our all,” shared SANI.

The band’s set included ‘Amplify’, the title track from their first full-length album, EVOLVE. Slower moments saw fans light up the venue with their phone flashlights, but as the band shifted back into their up-tempo material, the room quickly turned into a sea of cheering and jumping fans.

One song in particular brought Berlin and CATCH THE YOUNG together: their cover of German singer Nena’s ‘99 Luftballons’. Taking on the local favourite drew an especially enthusiastic response from the audience, turning the familiar ‘80s hit into one of the night’s standout moments.

The performance also gave the group another opportunity to bring their alternative pop-rock sound beyond Korea, with their vocal harmonies and full-band arrangements at the centre of the set.

“It was a great opportunity for us to perform at K-INDIE ON FESTIVAL. I'm proud of all our members,” said JUNGMO.

Berlin is only the beginning of the band’s latest international run. CATCH THE YOUNG are next set to embark on their first Latin American tour, CATCH THE YOUNG LIVE EVOLVE: LATAM TOUR 2026, named after EVOLVE. The tour will take the band to Mexico City, Puerto Rico, Buenos Aires, and Santiago, giving even more fans a chance to experience their "YOUTH-POP ROCK" sound live.

Following previous editions in Latin America and Asia, the festival will make its worldwide expansion with six cinematic experiences featuring BTS, SEVENTEEN, TOMORROW X TOGETHER, and ENHYPEN, alongside an interactive 3D cheering party bringing together music from across the HYBE roster.
items.body:
K-pop is taking over the big screen this October. Trafalgar Releasing and HYBE have announced HYBE CINE FEST 2026, a week-long global cinema event running from 24 to 31 October across more than 60 territories.

Following previous editions in Latin America and Asia, the festival will make its worldwide expansion with six cinematic experiences featuring BTS, SEVENTEEN, TOMORROW X TOGETHER, and ENHYPEN, alongside an interactive 3D cheering party bringing together music from across the HYBE roster.

At the centre of the programme are two live viewing broadcasts from BTS WORLD TOUR ‘ARIRANG’. Fans can catch the group's first-ever performance in Argentina with BTS WORLD TOUR ‘ARIRANG’ IN BUENOS AIRES: LIVE VIEWING on 24 October in the Americas and 25 October for the rest of the world.

The festival will close with BTS WORLD TOUR ‘ARIRANG’ IN SÃO PAULO: LIVE VIEWING, broadcasting the finale of the group's Latin American tour on 30 October in the Americas and 31 October elsewhere.

CARATs, MOAs, and ENGENEs will also have their turn in front of the big screen. The lineup includes concert films SEVENTEEN WORLD TOUR 'NEW_', TOMORROW X TOGETHER WORLD TOUR 'ACT : TOMORROW', and ENHYPEN WORLD TOUR 'BLOOD SAGA'.

Rounding out the programme is HYBE CHEERING PARTY (IN 3D), an interactive cinema experience where fans can chant, sing along with 3D-enhanced lyrics, and bring out their official light sticks.

The screening will feature music videos from BTS, SEVENTEEN, TOMORROW X TOGETHER, ENHYPEN, LE SSERAFIM, &TEAM, BOYNEXTDOOR, TWS, ILLIT, KATSEYE, aoen, CORTIS, and SANTOS BRAVOS.

Select cinemas will also host Special Location experiences. Special Location Plus venues will feature interactive zones, official merchandise, and limited-edition capsule toys, while Special Location cinemas will offer photo zones and message walls. Dedicated HYBE CINE FEST Stores will also pop up at selected locations with official merchandise and capsule toys.

Tickets go on sale worldwide on 30 September, 6 AM PT / 9 AM ET / 2 PM BST. The BTS Live Viewing broadcasts will be anchored to specific live and delay-broadcast times (available at www.btsliveviewing.com). Full venue details are available at hybecinefest.com.

items.album: Tony Njoku ~ A World of Bodies on Fire
items.excerpt: Tony Njoku‘s recent work has moved between open-ended instrumental composition and song. A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE continues this movement in a more intimate setting. Across four pieces, piano, synthesisers and space provide the foundations of the music. items.body: Tony Njoku‘s recent work has moved between open-ended instrumental composition and song. A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE continues this movement in a more intimate setting. Across four pieces, piano, synthesisers and space provide the foundations of the music. The title track establishes the EP’s sound through layers of synthesiser harmonies that gather pace but stop short of a conventional climax. “Streams and Storms” turns towards private reflection, while “The Quiet Chaos of Playing It Safe” holds onto its tension without seeking a dramatic release. “Etude No. 1” strips the music down again, bringing the record to a sombre close. As Njoku explains in the accompanying interview, his move away from language is connected to an interest in how music can communicate feelings before they have been organised into words. Grief, exhaustion and recovery remain unresolved, expressed through harmony, resonance, dynamics and space. Small harmonic changes assume greater significance within these sparse arrangements. This is no suite in four movements, with constrasting character and same key signature. A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE is a protean EP that searches and digs inwards, taking unexpected turns without any desire to dazzle. There is no show-off moment, no virtuoso display demanding attention, nor any grand moment of portending grief; emotion remains understated and kept in check. The music is unafraid of intimacy, allowing sustained harmonies, shifts in density and silence to determine its course, leaving much of the experience behind these compositions unspoken. To help us put out the fire we reached out directly to Tony Njoku for an interview conducted via email. All Our Knives Are Always Sharp was a large-scale collaborative statement concerned with spiritual preparedness, cultural resistance and collective survival, while the Bloom releases increasingly embraced instrumental composition, chamber arrangements and themes of grief, memory and renewal. A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE feels like a further step in that direction: intensely personal, largely wordless and driven by the need to work through difficult emotions rather than narrative. Do you see this EP as the culmination of a journey that began with those recent releases, or did it emerge from a fundamentally different place? I don’t think of it as a culmination so much as another point of arrival. Each project tends to emerge from whatever questions I’m living with at the time. All Our Knives… was very outward-facing. It was about community, about bringing different voices into conversation around ideas of resilience and collective memory. Bloom and the instrumental work that followed became quieter spaces where I could sit with loss, change and the slower work of transformation. A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE came from an even more internal place. I wasn’t trying to tell a story or resolve anything. I was more interested in documenting a state of being and exorcising some pent-up feelings that were essentially causing me harm. The music became a way of staying present with difficult emotions rather than translating them into language. In that sense it feels connected to the recent releases, but I wasn’t consciously trying to complete a trilogy or close a chapter. It simply became the form those experiences needed. One of the recurring threads across recent works—from The Loops (Grief) and Looking For Light to the standalone single “Malaise”—is an engagement with emotional turbulence that is neither entirely despairing nor entirely hopeful. The title track of A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE speaks of moving through fire rather than escaping it. Has your understanding of grief, burnout and recovery changed over the course of these releases, and do you think this EP arrives at a different emotional destination than those earlier works? I think grief has become less about something to overcome and more about something you learn to live alongside. Earlier work probably carried a stronger desire to find resolution or to move towards the light. I don’t think I see it that way anymore. Recovery isn’t linear, and neither is burnout. There are moments of joy inside exhaustion and moments of uncertainty inside healing. The image of moving through fire rather than escaping it felt important because some experiences can’t be bypassed. They change you. The music on this EP isn’t trying to extinguish the fire; it’s trying to understand what remains after you’ve passed through it. If there’s hope here, it’s a quieter kind. It’s found in endurance, attention and the possibility of continuing to create despite everything. One of the striking aspects of All Our Knives Are Always Sharp was the way you brought together an extraordinary community of Black British voices—Tricky, GAIKA, Ghostpoet, Coby Sey, James Massiah, Space Afrika, Labi Junior and others—creating a record that felt simultaneously personal and collective. More broadly, your recent work has moved freely between songs, spoken-word collaborations, chamber-like compositions, ambient electronics and abstract instrumental forms. By contrast, A WORLD OF BODIES ON FIRE feels almost entirely self-contained, built around piano, synthesisers and extended instrumental pieces. After such a collaborative album, did the absence of other voices create a different kind of honesty or vulnerability? Collaboration has always been fundamental to my practice because it allows ideas to exist beyond my own perspective. All Our Knives… couldn’t have existed without those voices. The conversations between people were the point of the record. With this EP I found myself needing the opposite experience. I needed solitude, not because I wanted to withdraw from community, but because I needed to hear what was underneath all the noise. Working mostly alone meant there was nowhere to hide. Every hesitation, every silence, every decision belonged to me. That can feel vulnerable, but it can also be very freeing because you’re no longer trying to explain yourself through words or through other people’s interpretations. I also needed space to cry and I find that’s a hard thing for me to do in front of people, I let go of my masks the most in solitude. So it became a conversation with the instruments themselves. The piano, synthesizers and space all became collaborators in a different sense. You’ve described this EP as a collection of “raging exhalations, quiet revelations, subtle smirks of humility, laments and meditations.” Unlike many of your previous releases, there are no guest vocalists, no lyrics and no obvious narrative anchors. Did working without words feel liberating or exposing? And at this stage in your career, do you feel instrumental music has become just as capable as song of carrying the political, spiritual and emotional concerns that have always been central to your work? Working without words was both liberating and exposing. Lyrics can sometimes direct people towards a particular meaning, whereas instrumental music leaves much more room for the listener’s own experience. That openness was something I wanted to embrace. I’ve become increasingly interested in what music communicates before language enters. Breath, texture, resonance, silence… these things carry meaning too. They can hold emotion in ways that words sometimes can’t. I don’t really separate instrumental music from song anymore. They’re just different ways of asking the same questions. The political, spiritual and emotional concerns that have always interested me don’t disappear when language disappears. They become embodied differently. Sometimes a sustained note or a shift in harmony can express something that would become smaller if I tried to explain it. (Gianmarco Del Re)

items.album: Here Because of Hope
items.tags: experimental electronic jazz world psych prog
items.excerpt: Ezra Collective Here Because of Hope Their fourth album asks why so much Black music born from pain makes people dance. items.album: The Forest Beneath Language: Entering the World of György Kurtág in Marlboro
items.excerpt: (Photo credit: Allen Cohen) Reaching Marlboro requires a gradual surrender of scale. Roads narrow, familiar coordinates loosen, and the forest exerts its own editorial influence, stripping away whatever feels extraneous until distance becomes a form of concentration. items.body: (Photo credit: Allen Cohen) Reaching Marlboro requires a gradual surrender of scale. Roads narrow, familiar coordinates loosen, and the forest exerts its own editorial influence, stripping away whatever feels extraneous until distance becomes a form of concentration. On September 20, 2026, that concentration gathered inside Ragle Hall at the Serkin Center, where the Marlboro Music Artist Residency Program presented The World of György Kurtág, an arresting sequence of works composed or arranged for soprano and double bass. Beyond the hall stood the wooded seclusion of southern Vermont; within it, soprano Lucy Fitz Gibbon and bassist William Langlie Miletich moved between Sprechstimme, art song, extended technique, and charged silence. Seclusion mattered because Kurtág’s music alters the proportions of attention. The claim embedded in the program’s title was stranger than its apparent simplicity suggested. The phrase “world of” ordinarily announces breadth, an oeuvre surveyed from above. Kurtág offers no such cartographic comfort. His world emerges through radical compression, forming under pressure between a sound and its possible disappearance. A few pitches can contain the moral weight of a dramatic scene. A pause can bend duration until time folds inward, secreting another time inside itself. His miniatures remain small only to the clock. To enter them is to accept unfamiliar laws under which fragments carry the mass of vanished wholes and inhalation behaves as active matter. The surrounding forest supplied an uncannily precise grammar for this experience. Every trunk concealed years in concentric script; every root continued a sentence underground. Kurtág’s art operates within a related economy of the imperceptible. A phrase ends, yet its pressure travels elsewhere. Music becomes the audible extremity of processes occurring beneath language. The sequence approached that hidden economy gently through Lembit Beecher’s With Grandchildren, drawn from his 2014 cycle Looking at Spring: Meditations on Aging. The larger work grew from interviews librettist Liza Balkan conducted with senior citizens in Toronto and central Vermont, making its appearance in Marlboro feel almost homeward. Their voices had passed into text and music before returning to the region transformed, bearing traces of their speakers without claiming to preserve them intact. Harmonics in the bass courted a rocking motion whose comfort never became secure, while Fitz Gibbon searched amid the delicate failures of memory. The soul became an unfinished sentence poised beneath scissors, family albums reduced to particles of touch and chronology. Bone creaked as marrow acquired a secret literacy, becoming a divining instrument for the inaccessible past. Beecher respected recollection as an unstable act in which forgetting shapes experience as decisively as retention. Miletich’s pale overtones gave the bass an elderly nervous system of its own. The final word escaped capture, suspending language where recognition touches disappearance. John Cage’s The Wonderful Widow of Eighteen Springs opened another passage into that borderland. Composed in 1942, its text comes from a nocturnal passage concerning Isobel in Finnegans Wake, a book of sleeping consciousness and linguistic mutation. Cage answered that abundance with severe economy. The voice circles within three pitches, while the original accompaniment is played on a closed piano tapped by the player. In Marlboro, those impulses migrated to the double bass, where Miletich turned his instrument of choice into a hollow nocturnal chamber. What had once been struck wood surrounding dormant strings now came from an assemblage held against the player’s body, each impact becoming a coded knock from somewhere inside itself. Fitz Gibbon sustained Cage’s narrow compass with remarkable intensity. Repetition wandered in place, circling a road inferred from every failed attempt to leave it. James Joyce’s words acquired the phosphorescence of objects glimpsed among trees. Isobel became a consciousness translated into the landscape, as identity passed into leaf matter and the boundary between a sleeping mind and the forest dreaming it lost authority. Amy Beth Kirsten’s yes I said yes I will Yes followed as a second excavation of Joyce, drawing on Molly Bloom’s concluding monologue in Ulysses. Written in 2012 for soprano and contrabass, with the bassist also vocalizing, it entered an illuminating dialogue with Cage. Both composers extract a concentrated vocal world from Joyce’s literary machinery. Whereas Cage cools language toward incantation, Kirsten restores its heat while fracturing the body that generates it. Isobel’s suspension yields to Molly’s consciousness in bed, where memory moves through eros and resistance before reaching the irrevocable “Yes.” Fitz Gibbon and Miletich rendered that sensuality as a condition divided against itself. Pizzicato entered beside Miletich’s droning hum, while glissandi bent the music from stable coordinates. Fitz Gibbon inhabited desire while observing its mechanisms from afar, consciousness hovering above its own flesh. The deeply inflected conclusion unfolded as slow-motion blues, each pitch bearing the drag of pleasure becoming memory before experience could have its say. These works prepared the ear for Kurtág’s Einige Sätze aus den Sudelbüchern Georg Christoph Lichtenbergs, Op. 37a, begun in 1996 and expanded for soprano and double bass in 1999. The cycle arose from his encounter with the private notebooks of Georg Christoph Lichtenberg, the 18th-century physicist whose intellect moved between experiment and satire. Never intended for publication, these “waste books” gathered observations whose brevity sharpened their reach. Lichtenberg’s scrutiny ranges across provincialism and religion, colonialism and literary history. Each joke becomes a trapdoor opening onto centuries of vanity. Kurtág began setting the aphorisms while ill, initially for solo soprano. Singer Maria Husmann encouraged the addition of double bass after experimenting with improvised accompaniment, a genesis audible in the finished cycle. Voice and instrument discover one another without settling into fixed roles. The bass accompanies before interrupting, then places a dark question mark beneath Lichtenberg’s wit. Fitz Gibbon and Miletich inhabited these relations with theatrical aptitude. The opening “Die Kartoffeln” (“The Potatoes”) was oddly beautiful in its evocation of slumbering tubers and their potential afterlife. “Kirchtürme” (“Church Spires”) rose through lovely pizzicato, its aspiration destabilized by the plucking that produced it. “Koan” became a fervent prayer edging toward cognitive seizure. Kurtág exposed the nervous system inside each of these, revealing the involuntary twitch beneath polished intelligence. That method reached sardonic clarity in “…und eine neue Welt…” (“…and a New World…”), where Fitz Gibbon sang through her teeth: “The American who discovered Columbus made a nasty discovery.” The reversal compresses colonial history into a grammatical ambush, exposing discovery as a story power tells about intrusion. Here, as elsewhere in the cycle, language appeared to turn against the assumptions concealed within its own syntax. Beecher’s stop-motion films, still a work in progress and therefore accompanying only selected aphorisms, extended this instability into a visual register. His reappearance as animator also gave the program a satisfying circular architecture. Having entered through his own music in With Grandchildren, he returned within Kurtág’s, translating acts of listening into movement and matter. Objects advanced through minute discontinuities, their apparent motion created by absences between frames. The art form therefore proved uncannily suited to Kurtág, whose music repeatedly asks the listener to construct continuity across charged gaps. Both forms make disappearance part of their syntax. The most persuasive union of image and sound came in “Ein Liebhaber der klassischen Philologie” (“A Classical Philology Aficionado”), concerning a man so enamored of Homer that he reads the German angenommen as “Agamemnon.” Books towered behind drifting clouds while statues looked on as thought acquiring mineral flesh. Beecher let the visual analog unfold slowly, giving the words time to expose the strange pathology hidden inside cultivated learning. Erudition became a benign haunting, a possession so complete that antiquity rewrote the present from within. The sequence clarified what the animations contributed to the cycle as a whole: they gave Kurtág’s microscopic dramas another surface upon which to misremember and mutate. The closing “Ein merkwürdiger Gedanke” (“A Strange Thought”) brought Kurtág’s humor to its darkest edge. Miletich and Fitz Gibbon allowed laughter to reveal its ancient kinship with fear. By then, one work had entered another through hidden roots. Cage’s knocks survived inside Kirsten’s tapping, while Beecher’s elderly voices continued inside Lichtenberg’s posthumous sentences. And through it all, Joyce’s sleeping forest returned in the Vermont woods surrounding the hall. The program cohered through subterranean recurrence, with each composition sending material below the surface for another to absorb. Marlboro’s seclusion ultimately changed the concert. Isolation became an acoustic form of relation, concentrating distant minds into one chamber. Beneath our feet, roots continued their exchanges without witnesses, each message altered by the body carrying it. The afternoon suggested that memory follows the same obscure traffic. We imagine ourselves as its custodians, although the reverse may lie closer to the truth. Memory could be the larger organism, ancient and unfinished, using each of us as a temporary organ through which to migrate. For one hour in Ragle Hall, voices became gills in that organism. The post The Forest Beneath Language: Entering the World of György Kurtág in Marlboro appeared first on Sequenza21.

items.body: Black Sherif takes his own sound apart on SUN SHERIF, the six-track EP he released through Blacko Management and EMPIRE in early September. The Konongo-born singer and rapper calls it “a deconstruction of everything Black Sherif’s done sonically“, a method that gives him the obsession he says he needs when working through fifteen or twenty demos at a time. That sound took shape on the “First Sermon” and “Second Sermon” singles of 2021, Twi verses set over highlife melody and UK drill drums, and in 2022 “Kwaku the Traveller” carried it to number one on Apple Music in Ghana and Nigeria. Two albums followed, The Villain I Never Was in 2022 and Iron Boy in April 2025. The EP brings in the Ghanaian singer AratheJay on “Forever” and the Trinidadian production duo Full Blown on “Love Again”, and Sherif sings “Jolie” alone, moving between Twi and English towards a chorus built on the French word for pretty. The verses are made of small acts of devotion: a New Year’s drive to her door, songs written for her in the manner of Kurt Cobain, a habit dropped because she disliked it. items.body: Review by memowakeman — Review originally posted at www.therocktologist.comAn outstanding album. The Chilean ensemble Asceta has established itself as one of those collectives you simply have to know if you are a fan of music made with extraordinary care and musicianship. Guided by the creative spirit of Rodrigo Maccioni, the band delivers an album in 2026 that, although there are still several months left in the year, could very well be considered the best Rock in Opposition and avant-prog release of the year. "The Fool Leading The Blind" is the title of the Chileans' third full-length release, an ambitious album that, across fifty three minutes, offers five compositions in which magic, social criticism, and music of the highest caliber take center stage. Everything begins with the album's title track, a twenty one minute suite that can be ominous at times, frenetic at others, and remarkably calm in between. The first three minutes are somewhat contemplative, as something gradually begins to take shape. Strings and drums establish a semi-slow rhythm that slowly builds until, around the four minute mark, the first explosion of rock arrives. Rock in Opposition, indeed, because the criticism directed toward our world and our politics is implicit throughout the piece, and the musicians express it through their constantly shifting yet remarkably intelligent way of communicating. I love the unexpected rhythmic changes, the moments when the energy and pulse suddenly rise, and the way every instrument introduces its own notes and ideas before converging into an incredibly solid composition that eventually leads us toward ecstasy. There is something beautiful about the way these musicians organize themselves to construct their music. I only wish that, as a society, we could demonstrate this same kind of organization when it comes to confronting bad governments and defending our land. After this emotional roller coaster, Asceta offers us the somber "Temple of Mirrors". Its opening minute is somewhat dissonant, with scattered sounds appearing here and there without any clearly defined form. Then, little by little, a structure begins to emerge, bringing clearer sounds and direction. Progressive music, naturally, but also classical music, an endless palette of colors and textures, and a remarkable convergence between acoustic and electric elements, as beautifully demonstrated by the guitar. Strings introduce the creepy and ominous atmosphere of "When They Arrive". Gradually, instruments such as bassoon, drums, and clarinet join the landscape, creating a dark environment in which a sense of unease comes naturally. There are brief bursts of intensity that could easily startle an unsuspecting listener, but there are also moments of harmony in which we can look around and decide which path to take. This is highly visual music, and every listen can inspire completely different stories in the listener's mind. There are passages that evoke After Crying or Art Zoyd. Wonderful. With "Everything Stopped", a frenetic and semi-chaotic rhythm takes over, constantly contrasted by pauses filled with cadence but also nervous energy. The ensemble creates fascinating musical connections. At times the strings take the spotlight, at others the winds or the drums, yet there is always a beautiful cohesion that serves as the thread connecting their performances. The music here is never linear, and that may initially turn away listeners who are not comfortable with such an approach. But once you connect with it, a genuine synergy develops, and it remains intact until the very end of the album. Speaking of endings, this magnificent record concludes with "Memento Mori", a ten minute composition that is colorful and multifaceted, filled with playful changes that bring brightness while contrasting beautifully with darker passages. The bass establishes an ongoing conversation with the clarinet and oboe, and as usual, the Chileans deliver a dose of avant-garde music of the highest caliber, something no fan of this particular musical territory should overlook. A well deserved round of applause for Asceta, lovers of art and natural opposers by conviction. May their talent and passion continue to drive them toward creating music as rewarding as this.
